title: Chapter 53 – Elder Mu's Offer
html:
[Lin Clan – Old Hu]

Hu has been sober for seventy-three days, and the first thing he learns about it is how loud the world is.

It is not that the noise has grown. It is that for twelve years he has been listening to it through a warm wet cloth, and now the cloth is gone. The hammers are loud. The crows on the granary roof are loud. The long dull argument of the stream, running down the quarry road, is a thing he can hear from his bed, at three in the morning, in the dark, in every one of its separate voices. He has begun to name them. The deep one he calls the Magistrate. The little quick one that slips over the stones, he calls the Clerk.

He sits on the edge of the narrow cot in the little room behind the forge with his one hand pressed over his one good eye, and the smell of fresh-sawn pine in his nose, and listens to the Clerk tell the Magistrate a long boring story. He is trying to remember what he used to do at this hour. He used to drink. It was the only thing that took the place of everything else.

Seventy-three, he thinks. And a letter on the table.

It lies where he left it, on the rough pine board that serves as a desk, under a lump of slag. A single sheet. Good paper, pale and smooth, with a faint sheen like skin. It came last night, not by hawk, not by a runner, but laid on the sill of the forge window with a pebble on it, a small round one, quite ordinary, while he slept eight feet away. No one saw who left it. The guards at the gate did not hear a footfall. The old Warden of the lower yard, who is supposed to know every man on the hill by his gait, says he felt nothing at all.

A quiet man, Hu thinks. Always was.

He does not need to read it again. He has the five lines by heart.

My dear Hu.

It has been a long time. I hope you are well. I should like to see you, once, before the autumn, at the cairn where the old road meets the river. I shall be there at noon, on the ninth day. I will come alone. You may bring whom you like.

I have something to give you. I think you have waited for it a long while.

Mu.

* * *

He tells them at breakfast, because he is too old to do otherwise.

It is a small gathering. The Patriarch, and his wife, and the boy, sitting round the low table in the Patriarch's study, with a pot of millet and a dish of pickled greens, and the morning sun on the floor. They have the look of people who have been awake a long time. Wenshi is not there; he is in the guardhouse, with a splint, drilling a dozen men who can barely lift a spear. The boy is eating steadily and says nothing. His pet, or whatever she is, sits at his elbow, with her whole round body shaped like a question.

Hu puts the letter down in the middle of the table, beside the bowl of greens.

"It came last night," he says.

Nobody touches it.

"I know the hand," he says. "It is the one that wrote the first note, the one you found under the cairn, Wenyuan. A scribe's. It is not Mu's own. He does not write his own letters. He has never in his life done a thing with his own hand that another man could do for him." He sits, heavily, on a stool. "But this one he signed. Look. The last line. The M. It has a little hook on the stem. He did that when he was young. I used to tell him it was affected."

"You knew him," says the Patriarch, very quietly.

"I did."

"You said that, in the spring. You said he was a man who had once taught you a thing."

"I said a great many things in the spring." Hu rubs his face. "It was not the whole of the truth. I did not wish to say the whole of it, with a knife at my back." He looks at the table. "I would like to say it now."

Qinghe pours him tea. It is a small, kind, ordinary act. He takes it in his one hand, and holds it, and finds that the hand is shaking.

"I was twenty-six," says Hu, "when I joined the Veiled Forge. He was already past thirty. He was not yet Elder Mu. He was a clerk, in the Sect's outer ledger-house, with ink on his cuffs and a gentle way with the junior disciples. He used to bring me tea. I was a hot-headed young fool, and the Forge was the most famous workshop in the east, and he, a boy with a limp and a stoop and a head full of Coral Gate script, was the only man in the whole of that vast loud place who would sit beside me at the furnace and ask me what I was doing."

"He liked you."

"He loved me. It is not the same thing." The tea has cooled. He does not drink. "He taught me to read the old script. It is a hard one. He said, Hu, you have the hands of a master and the eyes of a child. Learn to read, and you will make a thing that no one has ever made. I did. I made a great many. And all the while, in the little ledger-house, in the dark, he was learning another thing. He was learning what the Coral Gate was for."

"And what was it for?"

"It was a lock." Hu's voice is very dry. "It was always a lock. The Sect of the Pool, in the days before it was the Blood Shadow, had a Founder, and the Founder had a vault. The vault was sealed. Nobody has ever said what is in it, because nobody has ever opened it. But Mu had read the old rolls, and he came to believe that the whole of the Sect's power, the long slow blood, the Pool, the Well, the Rill, was only a key. Something to be used by whoever was strong enough to turn it."

"And you made the lock-picks."

"I made the Veiled Forge's masterwork." He smiles, bitterly. "I thought I was making a sword."

There is a long silence.

"He left," says Hu. "The year the Forge fell. We had a quarrel about it, a bad one. He said that the sword was a key, and I said that a sword was a sword. He took the old script and went into the dark. I took the drink." He sets down the cup. "I have not seen him in twenty-one years."

"And now he writes."

"And now he writes."

The sun lies on the floor. Outside the study, in the yard, a child is laughing at something. The sound is high and sweet and perfectly ordinary.

"Hu," says the boy, from the end of the table. His voice is level. "What is it that he thinks you've waited for?"

The old man looks at him for a long time.

"I think," he says, "that he means to offer me my arm."

* * *

They argue about it for an hour. It is not an argument. It is a sort of slow, heavy, careful weighing, in which every word is picked up and set down again like a piece of china. The Patriarch is for refusing. The mother is for going, with a dozen guards on the ridge. The boy says nothing at all. He sits with his hands in his lap and his small pale eyes going from one face to the next, and when at last they all fall silent, he says only:

"It is a trap."

"Naturally," says Hu.

"Then why go?"

"Because he wants me to. And a man who wants a thing will sometimes tell you what it is, if you give him the chance." Hu looks at him. "I have been afraid of Mu for forty years, boy. I should like to find out whether I am right."

"It is a poor reason."

"It is the only one I have."

The boy considers him. Then, with the tiny gesture of one who has set down a heavy bag, he nods.

"I will be on the ridge," he says. "With the Echo. If he moves, I will know."

"You will do nothing of the kind," says Qinghe sharply.

"I will do nothing," says Jian, "except listen. That is all I do." A pause. "It is not much, Mother. It is only an ear."

She looks at him. After a time, with the faint air of a woman who has lost an argument she did not know she was in, she lifts her hand and lets it fall.

* * *

The cairn stands where the Salt Road meets the river, a rough heap of gray stones, waist-high, with a rusted iron ring set into the top. It is the oldest thing in the valley. Nobody knows who built it. It was there when the Lins came up the road, and the clan has hung ribbons on it for four hundred years, in the old way, for the dead and the travelers.

It is almost noon. The river is slow and brown and wide. The air shimmers over the stones. Under a bleached white willow, ten paces from the cairn, a man is sitting on a folding stool with a small clay jar on his knee.

He rises as Hu comes down the bank.

He has not changed. That is the first shock. Hu had thought, in some secret corner of himself, that there would be signs, that twenty-one years would have worn something away: the stoop, the limp, the long sad gentle face. There is nothing. The man is eighty-two, and looks forty-five. He wears a plain gray scholar's robe, with ink on his cuff. His hair is black. His hands are very clean.

"Hu," says Mu.

"Mu."

"You are sober." The soft voice is full of warm delight. "I had heard, but I did not believe. I am so glad. It becomes you." He lifts the clay jar. "I have brought tea. It is the old kind. You may remember it."

"I do."

"Then sit."

Hu sits. The willow is cool, and the grass under it is deep and fragrant, and he has the odd feeling, as he lowers himself onto the stool, that he is twenty-six, and a little drunk on his own cleverness, and that the world is an ordinary place.

That, he thinks, is how he does it.

* * *

They drink. It is the same tea. It is bitter and green and faintly sweet, with a taste like crushed leaves. It has the power, which he had forgotten, of making a man feel entirely safe.

"You look well," says Mu.

"I look like a corpse."

"A well-kept one." The Elder smiles. "You have your color back. You stand straight. You have, I think, stopped being so angry. It was the anger I was sorry for. I used to lie awake and think of it, in the cell. I thought: it will kill him. And it nearly did."

"Not the anger," says Hu. "The drink."

"They are the same river." Mu sets down his cup. "I did not come to talk of that. I came to give you a gift."

"Ah."

"You will not like it."

"I do not like most things."

"It is this." The Elder reaches into his sleeve, and draws out a small flat package wrapped in black silk. He lays it on his knee, unwraps it, and holds it out in two hands.

It is an arm.

Not a real one. It is a thing of pale bone and dark thread, a limb the length of a man's forearm, jointed at the elbow, with a hand at the end of it like the hand of a statue. It is exquisitely made. The fingers are articulated. The joints glisten. In the white light of noon it looks almost alive, and where it ends, at the upper edge, a thin delicate lattice of fine silver wire runs out like the roots of a tree.

"It is a Rill-stage prosthesis," says Mu, gently. "It took six years. The bone is from a spirit-ape, the thread from the Sect's own silkworms. It will take a Qi channel, if you wish to give it one. It will do whatever you tell it. It will hold a hammer. It will turn a crucible." He smiles. "It will make you whole."

Hu looks at it. His mouth is quite dry. For a moment he does not trust himself to speak, and when he does, the voice that comes out is a croak.

"How long have you had it?"

"Eleven years."

"For me?"

"I never made anything for anyone else." Mu's eyes are very kind. "I knew where you were. I always knew. I used to send a man, to see how you did. He said you had gone to a hill in the east, and lived in a granary, and that you lost an arm in a fire. I thought: I did not even know he would need it. And I began to build." The soft voice trembles, very slightly. "You will think it is a bribe. It is not. It is only a gift. I would give it to you if you said no to everything else. I should like you to know that."

Hu looks at the arm. He looks at it for a very long time. In the long grass at his feet a cricket has begun to sing.

Eleven years, he thinks. Eleven years, and he never once sent a word.

"And the rest?" he says. "The everything else?"

"The rest is small." Mu folds the silk. "I should like you to come and work for me. For a season. There is a book you carry, the first volume of the Hundred Veins. And a pangolin, which I do not carry. And a door, which neither of us do. It is a very simple matter. You make a key. I use it. And in the end, when it is over, I give you this, and the Veiled Forge, and a sum of money, and you are free to go wherever you please."

"And the clan?"

"Will be left alone."

"As the Lin were left alone at the Narrows?"

For the first time, a thin shadow crosses the gentle face. "That was regrettable. It was my pupil's doing. I had not intended it to go so far." He sighs. "I am an old man, Hu. I do not like a fuss. I only wish to do the one thing, and then sit in my garden."

"What thing?"

"My master," says Mu, "is dying."

It is a very quiet statement. It has no emphasis. He says it as a man says that it is raining. But Hu, who has known him fifty years and not seen him in twenty-one, hears something go through the soft voice like a crack through ice.

"He has been dying a long time. He is three hundred and twelve. He is a Rill, the last of the old line, and the vault is the only thing that can keep him. I do not ask you to love him. I ask only that you should understand. I have given my whole life to a single door. And I find, at the end of it, that I do not much care what is behind."

"That is a terrible thing to say."

"It is the only true thing I know."

* * *

Hu sits for a long time in the shade of the willow.

The river slides by. The sun climbs, and the shadows shorten, and somewhere across the water a heron lifts out of the reeds and goes up, slowly, with its legs trailing. He has the pale bone arm in his lap. He does not remember taking it. It lies against his knee, cool and smooth, like the arm of a sleeping child, and the long silver roots of its wire lie across his thigh.

He thinks of the boy.

He thinks of a gray-robed child in a granary, at midnight, with a roll of needles in his sleeve, saying in a perfectly level voice that he did not want to kill anybody. He thinks of a woman who smelled of herbs, binding an old man's hand, and saying Hu, very gently, as one says a name. He thinks of a one-armed fool in a bent leather apron, who for ten years had been the clan's chief embarrassment, and who on the morning after the fire had woken to find forty people standing in a ring round the burned doorway, with buckets in their hands, not saying anything.

They did not ask me to be better, he thinks. They only put out the fire.

"No," says Hu.

Mu does not move.

"I beg your pardon?"

"I said no. I am obliged to you for the arm. It is a very fine piece of work. It is the finest I have ever seen, and I include my own." He sets it down on the grass, with care, on its square of silk. "But I will not wear it."

"Hu—"

"I will tell you why, because you were my friend." He lifts his eyes. The one clear dark one is steady and bright. "I do not want to be whole. I have been whole, and I was a fool. I have been broken, and I was a drunk. I find that I have been, for a season, something else. I do not have a name for it. It is the thing you are when you stop being afraid." His voice shakes. "I like it. I should like to keep it a while."

"A refiner does not belong in a hill."

"I am not a refiner. I am a man who lights a fire in a shed, for people who have nothing, and is paid in porridge." He smiles. It is a ruined, crooked, wonderful smile, like a door left open in a ruin. "It is the best work I ever did."

Mu says nothing. The gentle face has gone quite blank. It is, Hu thinks, the blankness of a man who has just heard a sentence in a language he used to know and cannot, for a moment, recall the meaning of.

"You are making a mistake," says the Elder, at last.

"Very probably."

"I could have made them give you the arm. I could have made them give you everything. I do not like to take what I can ask for." He rises. His robe falls straight. "But I will take it, Hu. In the end. I will take the book, and the beast, and the door. I will take the hill, if I must. You understand that. It is not a threat. It is only the order of things."

"I understand it."

"I am sorry."

"I know you are. It is the worst thing about you."

Mu bows, very slightly. He turns. He goes up the bank, with the clay jar in his hand and his shoulders a little bowed, a lean gray figure under the glaring noon, and for a moment Hu thinks he will say nothing more.

Then, at the top of the slope, he stops, and half turns, and speaks without looking back.

"The little one in the boy's sleeve. The seamwalker." His voice is mild. "She has lost three scales. Did you know?"

Hu does not answer.

"Three. I can feel the places. They are cold and bare, like windows in a house. A seamwalker with six scales is a thing that can do almost anything. A seamwalker with three, I find, is a thing that wants looking after." A small pause. "I should like to look after her. I think she would be better in my garden than on your hill."

"She is not yours to take."

"No. But she is a very small creature, and a very tired one." The soft voice is almost tender. "It is a great pity, I think, that a child should have to carry so much."

He goes.

Hu sits where he is, in the long hot grass, with the arm on its square of black silk at his feet and the river running slow and brown beside him. A cricket sings. A faint breeze stirs the willow. He does not move for a long time.

Then, very slowly, with his one hand, he takes up the silk and folds it over the pale bone, and wraps it, and sets it in the crook of his knee. He will give it to the boy, he thinks. He will say, burn it. He will say, do not touch it. He will say that it is the most beautiful thing he has ever held.

He will not say that he wept.

* * *

He finds the boy at the top of the bank, in the dry fern, lying flat with his palms to the ground.

Jian does not look up. His face is the color of tallow. A thin line of dried blood runs from one nostril to his lip. He has been listening, Hu realizes, for a very long hour, on the thread of the Echo, with the whole of his small body bent to a place two hundred paces away. He has heard every word. Not the sound of it, perhaps, but the shape. The long soft pauses. The stillness at the end.

"You said no," says Jian.

"I did."

"Why?"

"I told you." Hu lowers himself onto a stone. His knees crack. "A man has to be something. I find I would rather be a fool in a granary than a whole man in a garden."

The boy nods, as if he had expected it. He turns his head, at last. His eyes are enormous and dark, with the faint gold ring shining round the black. "He knows about her. About Pebble. The three scales."

"He felt them. I do not know how. A seamwalker leaves a little of herself in every seam she opens, and a man who has made a key for forty years can taste it, I think, like salt on the wind." Hu sets the black silk bundle in the fern. "Do not touch that. It is an arm. It is the best I have seen. Burn it."

"I will."

"And do not let her out of your sight. Do you understand? Not for a morning. Not for a meal." The old man's voice is rough. "He does not threaten. When he says a thing is a pity, he has already decided what to do about it."

"I understand."

"Do you?"

Jian looks at the small pale creature beside him in the moss. She has curled into a ball, with her tail over her nose, and her scales are dull in the noon light. She is shaking. It is a fine, rapid, continuous tremor, like the shiver of a leaf.

I am not afraid, she says. He feels it, faint and high and thin, in the back of his skull. I am only very cold.

"Yes," says Jian, aloud, softly. "I understand."

He puts both hands round her. She is no bigger than a loaf, and no heavier. He lifts her to his chest, under his cloak, and holds her there, in the long hot silence, with the river running slow and brown below them and a cricket singing in the grass. He does not say anything else. He only holds on.
